When misfortune strikes, we instinctively demand explanations: Why me? What did I do wrong? Though fully aware that randomness largely dictates what happens in life, [[1]], we believe in a just world where good people are rewarded and bad people face consequences. This cognitive bias, known as the Just-World Fallacy, [[2]] that people get what they deserve, leading us to perceive life’s outcomes as fair rather than arbitrary.
The Just-World Hypothesis fosters harsh judgments and diminishes compassion. Socially, it fuels victim-blaming, suggesting that the misfortune was due to the victim’s [[3]]. It also reinforces systemic inequalities by justifying the status quo and resisting change. When people believe life is inherently fair, they may overlook structural injustices, convinced that those struggling simply don’t work hard enough. In personal relationships, this bias creates emotional detachment, making people less likely to offer support. It can even lead to self-blame, as those facing hardship may believe they are [[4]] responsible for their struggles, further deepening emotional distress.
To challenge this bias, developing empathy and recognizing the complexities of life’s outcomes are crucial. Perspective-taking—considering how circumstances shape others’ lives—can help, [[5]] can exposing ourselves to diverse viewpoints. It won’t be easy to accept that the world isn’t always fair, but doing so allows us to extend greater kindness to others and ourselves in times of hardship.

tags.topic: the Just-World Fallacy and its harmful effects
